lead: This unit treats a circuit with an input pair and an output pair of terminals as a black box described by four numbers. You learn the Z, Y, h, g and ABCD parameter sets, how to convert between them, how to combine two-ports in series, parallel and cascade, and how to test reciprocity and symmetry. The last chapter runs analysis backwards and builds LC and RC one-ports from a given impedance by the Foster and Cauer methods.
about: The unit starts with ports, the sign convention for the four port variables and the idea of a parameter set. Z and Y parameters come from open-circuit and short-circuit tests; hybrid (h and g) parameters mix the two and suit transistors; ABCD parameters handle cascades and terminated networks. A conversion table links all the sets, and the interconnection rules show when Z or Y matrices add and when ABCD matrices multiply. Reciprocity and symmetry tests then shorten the work, and network synthesis closes the unit. One T network of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 4 Ω is used in every chapter, so its numbers can be compared from set to set.

chapters.idea: A two-port is a linear network seen only through two terminal pairs; four external variables V1, I1, V2 and I2 describe it.
chapters.depth: Define port, one-port, two-port and multi-port; terminal pairs; sign convention: I1 enters port 1 and leaves its return, I2 enters port 2 and leaves its return; V1 and V2 are across the ports. A linear two-port needs two equations linking the four variables, so four parameters. No independent sources inside; initial stored energy zero. Mention applications: transistor, filter, transformer, transmission line. Some syllabi call it a quadripole or four-terminal network.

figure.aria: A block diagram shows port 1 on the left and port 2 on the right of a linear two-port, with V1, I1 and V2, I2 marked at the ports.

chapters.example: A two-port has V1 = 10 V, I1 = 2 A entering port 1, V2 = −4 V, I2 = 1 A entering port 2. Find the power entering the two-port. Answer: P = V1 I1 + V2 I2 = 10 × 2 + (−4) × 1 = 16 W.
chapters.trap: The sign of I2: it is defined entering port 2, so a load current leaving port 2 is −I2. A wrong sign flips the V2 I2 term.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: circuit elements and Kirchhoff's laws; Unit 2: Thevenin and Norton.
chapters.leave: Parameter definitions to 6.2–6.4; coupled coils and transformers to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Z parameters express V1 and V2 as a matrix times I1 and I2; Y parameters invert that relation.
chapters.depth: Define z11 = V1/I1 with I2 = 0 (port 2 open), z12 = V1/I2 with I1 = 0, z21 = V2/I1 with I2 = 0, z22 = V2/I2 with I1 = 0. Units ohms. Y = Z⁻¹; y11 = I1/V1 with V2 = 0 (port 2 short), and similarly y12, y21, y22. Units siemens. Show open-circuit and short-circuit tests. Z may not exist if its matrix is singular. Some syllabi call them open-circuit impedance and short-circuit admittance parameters.

figure.aria: The upper branch gives an open-circuit Z test; the lower branch gives a short-circuit Y test.

chapters.example: A T network has series arms Z1 = 2 Ω, Z2 = 3 Ω and shunt arm Z3 = 4 Ω. Find z11, z12, z21 and z22. Answer: z11 = Z1 + Z3 = 6 Ω, z12 = Z3 = 4 Ω, z21 = Z3 = 4 Ω, z22 = Z2 + Z3 = 7 Ω.
chapters.trap: z11 is not measured with port 2 shorted; Z parameters need an open-circuit test. Y parameters need a short-circuit test.
chapters.prereq: 6.1; Unit 1 Ohm's law and KVL/KCL; Unit 3 impedance.
chapters.leave: h/g and ABCD to 6.3 and 6.4; conversions to 6.5.

chapters.idea: h parameters use I1 and V2 as inputs and give V1 and I2; g parameters use V1 and I2 as inputs and give I1 and V2.
chapters.depth: Write V1 = h11 I1 + h12 V2; I2 = h21 I1 + h22 V2. Define h11 = V1/I1 with V2 = 0 (output short), h12 = V1/V2 with I1 = 0 (input open), h21 = I2/I1 with V2 = 0, h22 = I2/V2 with I1 = 0. Units: h11 Ω, h12 dimensionless, h21 dimensionless, h22 S. h21 is current gain; h12 is reverse voltage gain. Inverse hybrid: I1 = g11 V1 + g12 I2; V2 = g21 V1 + g22 I2; units g11 S, g12 dimensionless, g21 dimensionless, g22 Ω. h and g matrices are inverses. Some syllabi call h the hybrid parameters and g the inverse hybrid parameters.

figure.aria: I1 and V2 drive the two h-parameter equations; the upper path builds V1, the lower path builds I2.

chapters.trap: h11 is measured with the output shorted, not open; h12 and h21 are dimensionless, while h11 is ohms and h22 is siemens.
chapters.leave: Conversions to 6.5; transistor models to electronics courses.

chapters.idea: ABCD parameters relate input voltage and current to output voltage and current, so cascaded two-ports multiply their matrices.
chapters.depth: Use [V1; I1] = [[A, B], [C, D]] [V2; −I2] with I2 entering port 2. Define A = V1/V2 with I2 = 0 (output open), B = V1/(−I2) with V2 = 0 (output short), C = I1/V2 with I2 = 0, D = I1/(−I2) with V2 = 0. Units: A and D dimensionless, B Ω, C S. For a reciprocal network AD − BC = 1. For a symmetric network A = D. Cascade rule: ABCD = ABCD1 × ABCD2 in signal order. Some syllabi call them transmission or chain parameters.

figure.aria: In a cascade the chain matrices multiply from left to right.

chapters.example: Two two-ports are cascaded. The first has A1 = 2, B1 = 3 Ω, C1 = 1 S, D1 = 2. The second has A2 = 1, B2 = 0 Ω, C2 = 0.5 S, D2 = 1. Find the overall ABCD matrix. Answer: A = 2×1 + 3×0.5 = 3.5, B = 2×0 + 3×1 = 3 Ω, C = 1×1 + 2×0.5 = 2 S, D = 1×0 + 2×1 = 2. So ABCD = [[3.5, 3], [2, 2]].
chapters.trap: The minus sign on I2 in the ABCD definition is part of the convention. Without it, B and D change sign. Also matrix multiplication order matters.

chapters.idea: All parameter sets are different rearrangements of the same two linear equations, so you can convert between them by algebra.
chapters.depth: Cover a conversion table between Z, Y, h, g and ABCD. Define Δz = z11 z22 − z12 z21, Δy = y11 y22 − y12 y21, Δh = h11 h22 − h12 h21. Show one derivation, e.g. Z→ABCD: A = z11/z21, B = Δz/z21, C = 1/z21, D = z22/z21. Show Y→ABCD: A = −y22/y21, B = −1/y21, C = −Δy/y21, D = −y11/y21. Show h→ABCD: A = −Δh/h21, B = −h11/h21, C = −h22/h21, D = −1/h21. Conversion fails if the denominator is zero. Some syllabi call this interrelationships among parameter sets.

figure.aria: Every edge is a rearrangement; the divisor is the parameter in the denominator.

chapters.trap: A formula with z21, y21 or h21 in the denominator fails for a unilateral network where that parameter is zero. Do not use a conversion that does not exist.

chapters.idea: Series connection adds Z matrices, parallel connection adds Y matrices, and cascade multiplies ABCD matrices, provided the port conditions are met.
chapters.depth: Series: input ports in series and output ports in series, same port currents, voltages add, so Z = Z1 + Z2. Parallel: input ports in parallel and output ports in parallel, same port voltages, currents add, so Y = Y1 + Y2. Cascade: output of one feeds input of the next, so ABCD = ABCD1 × ABCD2. Check the port conditions: no circulating current in series, no circulating voltage in parallel. If the simple condition fails, use the general interconnection equations. Applications: filters, attenuators, transmission lines.

figure.aria: Each connection has one matrix rule; the rule is valid only when the port currents or voltages split as assumed.

chapters.example: Two identical two-ports, each with z11 = 6 Ω, z12 = 4 Ω, z21 = 4 Ω, z22 = 7 Ω, are connected in series at both ports. Find the combined Z matrix. Answer: Z = Z1 + Z2 = [[12, 8], [8, 14]] Ω.
chapters.trap: Do not add ABCD matrices in cascade; multiply them. Do not add Z matrices in parallel; convert to Y first or use the correct formula.
chapters.leave: Terminated input/output impedance to 6.7; conversions to 6.5.

chapters.idea: A reciprocal two-port has equal transfer parameters both ways; a symmetric two-port looks the same from either port.
chapters.depth: Reciprocity conditions: z12 = z21, y12 = y21, h12 = −h21, AD − BC = 1. Symmetry conditions: z11 = z22, y11 = y22, A = D; in h parameters Δh = h11 h22 − h12 h21 = 1. A symmetric passive linear network is reciprocal, but reciprocity alone does not imply symmetry. Use these to simplify the terminated two-port: input impedance Zin = z11 − z12 z21/(z22 + ZL); output impedance Zout = z22 − z12 z21/(z11 + ZS); voltage gain V2/V1 with load ZL. Mention one line that h parameters are used in negative-feedback amplifier analysis; detail goes to electronics.

figure.aria: Reciprocity is a transfer condition; symmetry is a port-interchange condition.

chapters.example: A T network has z11 = 6 Ω, z12 = 4 Ω, z21 = 4 Ω, z22 = 7 Ω. Test reciprocity and symmetry. Find Zin when a 3 Ω load is connected at port 2. Answer: z12 = z21 = 4 Ω, so it is reciprocal. z11 = 6 Ω ≠ z22 = 7 Ω, so it is not symmetric. Zin = 6 − 4×4/(7+3) = 6 − 1.6 = 4.4 Ω.
chapters.trap: Reciprocity is not symmetry. A reciprocal two-port can have z11 ≠ z22. Also the h reciprocity condition has a minus sign: h12 = −h21.
chapters.leave: Negative-feedback design to electronics courses; coupled coils to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Network synthesis asks whether a given driving-point impedance or admittance can be built from R, L and C, and if so, how.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Define driving-point impedance Z(s) and admittance Y(s). Positive-real function: real for real s, and Re Z(jω) ≥ 0 for all ω. LC one-port: Z(s) is a reactance function with simple poles and zeros alternating on the jω axis; residues positive. RC one-port: poles and zeros lie on the negative real axis and alternate; residues positive. Foster forms: partial-fraction expansion into series or parallel branches. Cauer forms: continued-fraction ladder by removing poles at infinity or zero. Show one Foster I LC example. Some syllabi call this network synthesis or realizability.

figure.aria: The tests differ by where poles and zeros lie; Foster and Cauer give two realization styles.

chapters.example: Test whether Z(s) = (s² + 1)/(s(s² + 4)) is an LC driving-point impedance. If yes, write its Foster I form and give element values. Answer: poles at 0 and ±j2; zeros at ±j1; they alternate. Partial fractions give Z(s) = 1/(4s) + (3/4) s/(s² + 4); residues are positive. Foster I is a 4 F capacitor in series with a parallel LC branch of L = 3/16 H and C = 4/3 F (normalized values with s in rad/s).
chapters.trap: Positive coefficients are not enough. For an LC function, poles and zeros must alternate on the jω axis and every residue must be positive. For an RC function, all critical frequencies must lie on the negative real axis.
chapters.prereq: Unit 5 Laplace transform and network functions; Unit 3 impedance; Unit 4 resonance.
chapters.leave: Filter approximation (Butterworth, Chebyshev) and active synthesis to other courses.
